archetype.name: Playoff Team (goaltending-first)
archetype.definition: A Dallas team whose standings position rests on elite goaltending, a top penalty kill and shot suppression, while its even-strength play is only league average and its offense has dropped well below its usual level.

report.headline: Oettinger and the penalty kill are carrying an offense that has gone quiet
report.take:
Dallas is 15-6-2, sixth on the site and second in a Central where Minnesota has started faster. The profile looks very different from recent Stars teams. For four straight seasons this club scored at a top-ten rate, ranking 3rd, 3rd and 9th in offense the last three years. This season it ranks 25th, at 2.83 goals a game against a league average of 3.2. It is winning because almost nobody scores on it. The Stars rank 3rd in goals allowed at 2.43 a game, 3rd in shots against at 24.1, and 3rd in penalty kill at 88.8%, well above the league's 77.2%.

The engine is Jake Oettinger. He is second of 72 on the goalie tab, with 12.3 goals saved above expected, a .909 save percentage and five shutouts in 18 starts. The team's 12.7 GSAx ranks 3rd, and the goaltending grade is an A+. This is not a fluke reading: the Stars' goalies posted 31.4 GSAx in 2024-25 and 15.9 last season. Behind him, Thomas Harley logs 25.57 minutes a night, ranks 3rd of 36 defensemen and has 15 points. The blueline grades a B overall because Esa Lindell's heavy minutes come with a .478 xGF share and a single point.

The numbers hide a team that is not winning the run of play. At 5-on-5 the Stars hold 50.1% of expected goals (17th) and 50% of shot attempts (16th), which is the middle of the league. Their 3 points beyond what the goal differential implies rank 4th. The five-game winning streak reads 2-0, 2-1 in overtime, 4-3 in overtime twice, then 1-0. That is excellent goaltending plus coin flips that all landed heads. The power play has also cooled to 21.4% (18th) from 28.6% a year ago.

Where it goes from here depends on the two sides of the ledger moving toward each other. The 114-point pace will not hold on these underlying numbers. Close-game luck fades, and even a great goalie rarely keeps this rate for a full season. The offense, though, has years of evidence that it is better than 25th. A team that keeps preventing goals at a top-five level and gets back to even an average attack is still a comfortable playoff club. That is the most likely path, just a less spectacular one than November suggests.

strengths.title: Oettinger is stealing games
strengths.body: Oettinger's 12.3 GSAx makes him the No. 2 goalie on the site and accounts for nearly all of the team's 12.7, which ranks 3rd. Dallas goaltending has been strongly positive in most recent seasons, so this is a real skill rather than a hot month. His exact rate will probably ease, but goaltending should stay a clear plus.

strengths.title: Elite penalty kill
strengths.body: At 88.8% the kill ranks 3rd and sits far above the league's 77.2%. Some of that is the goalie, since PK save rates swing on goaltending. Expect regression toward the low 80s, which is where Dallas has lived the last three seasons, but it should remain an asset.

strengths.title: Low shot volume against
strengths.body: Opponents get 24.1 shots on goal a game, 3rd fewest and below the league's 27. That structure keeps Oettinger's workload manageable. It is the most repeatable part of the defensive profile.

concerns.title: Offense has fallen off a cliff
concerns.body: Dallas ranks 25th in scoring at 2.83 goals a game, 0.37 below the league. That is a sharp break from top-ten offenses in each of the last three seasons. The power play has also slipped to 18th. Because the history says this group can score, some recovery is likely, but it has not shown up yet: the last five games produced only 2.6 goals a night.

concerns.title: Record ahead of the play
concerns.body: The 5-on-5 shares are dead average: 50.1% of expected goals and 50% of shot attempts. Meanwhile, 3 points above what the goal differential implies rank 4th. Three of the five straight wins came in overtime, and that kind of close-game fortune does not repeat reliably.

concerns.title: Centers find room against Dallas
concerns.body: Opposing centers produce 0.45 points a game against Dallas, above their expected 0.36, a 24th-ranked mark. They account for 39.1% of the points Dallas allows, against a league share of 27.6%. It is a 20-game sample, but it points to a middle of the ice that leans on the goalie.

trend.note: An 8-6 October gave way to a 7-2 November, and the Stars arrive on a five-game streak allowing 1.4 goals a game. The results are trending up faster than the underlying play, since the streak was built on one-goal and overtime finishes.

weekAhead.headline: Three division games against teams ranked below Dallas
weekAhead.body:
Every opponent this week sits below Dallas on the site (14th, 15th and 11th), and two of the three games are at home. Nashville is a mirror image: a strong goalie group (8.4 GSAx), the league's 2nd-best kill at 89.1%, and a points-over-goal-differential edge that ranks 5th. Nashville gets outshot badly, though, allowing 28.9 shots a game with a 47% shot-attempt share. Dallas should control territory and needs to finish.

The weekend is a back-to-back: at St. Louis on the 27th, then Utah at home on the 28th. St. Louis allows 29.6 shots a game (29th) and is riding a 13.3% shooting rate, which is the kind of opponent a quiet offense can get well against. Utah is the real test. Its 56.8% expected-goals share is 2nd in the league, and its 32.5% power play is 3rd. But its goalies sit at -10.3 GSAx (30th) and its kill is 27th, so Dallas should get chances to finish.

keyMatchups.title: Utah power play vs Dallas kill
keyMatchups.body: Utah converts 32.5% of its power plays, 3rd in the league, against a Dallas kill at 88.8%, 3rd. Whichever side wins this likely decides the final game of the week. With Utah driving play at 5-on-5, Dallas cannot afford to give it many chances.

keyMatchups.title: Dallas offense vs leaky goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Utah's save percentage is .878 (29th) and its penalty kill is 71.3% (27th). Utah also allows defensemen points above expectation, ranking 26th. That sets up well for Harley, who has 15 points and 5 on the power play. If Dallas cannot score here, the offensive slump is deeper than a cold spell.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume at St. Louis
keyMatchups.body: The Blues give up 29.6 shots a game and lean on a 103 all-situations PDO built on hot shooting. A low-event Dallas team should be able to tilt the shot count. With a back-to-back, Casey DeSmith (.906, 0.3 GSAx) may get one of these starts, which would narrow the goaltending edge.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Dallas scores more than twice a night against St. Louis and Utah, two defenses that allow volume or can't stop it, or keeps leaning on one-goal wins.

restOfSeason.body:
The 114-point pace is built on things that tend to fade: a 4th-ranked edge in close-game points, an 88.8% penalty kill, and a goalie saving goals at a near-league-best rate. At 5-on-5 Dallas is a .500 possession team. Expect the points rate to come down. The defensive identity should hold, though, because shot suppression is structural and Oettinger has a multi-year track record.

The offset is the offense. A 25th-ranked attack is out of character for a team that ranked 3rd, 3rd and 9th the last three years, so scoring should climb back toward league average. The likely result is a playoff team in the 100-to-110-point range, with the division seeding decided by whether the goals return before the save percentage cools.
swingFactors: Whether the offense and power play return to recent-season levels

confidence.note: 23 games in; goaltending has history behind it, but the scoring slump is a small sample.
